evidence: Plaut. Trin. 331: Quī eam perdidit?, of a man who has run through his fortune
terms.comment: The plain verb for money thrown away, as for time and effort (see “waste time”). With pecūniam it can also mean simply to lose money; the context tells. Of a waste of money as a loss, Traupman has jactūra.

evidence: Cic. Off. 2.55: pecūniās profundunt in eās rēs, quārum memoriam aut brevem aut nūllam omnīnō sint relictūrī
Cic. Rosc. Am. 6: per luxuriam effundere atque cōnsūmere

phrases.latin: faciat quidlubet: sūmat cōnsūmat perdat, dēcrētumst patī, dum illum modo habeam mēcum.
phrases.english: Let him do as he likes: let him take, spend, and waste; I’ve made up my mind to bear it, as long as I have him with me.

phrases.latin: prōdigī, quī epulīs … pecūniās profundunt in eās rēs, quārum memoriam aut brevem aut nūllam omnīnō sint relictūrī
phrases.english: spendthrifts, who pour out their money on feasts … on things of which they will leave a brief memory or none at all

phrases.latin: Tantī emere? Istud est pecūniam perdere.
phrases.english: Pay that much? That’s a waste of money.

phrases.latin: Nōlī nummōs tuōs in nūgās profundere.
phrases.english: Don’t waste your money on rubbish.

sources: Lewis & Short: perdo · Lewis & Short: profundo · Lewis & Short: effundo
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, p. 404.
